newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PMP SEE FUTURE PROFIT IMPROVEMENT.
newsitem.headline: PMP SEE FUTURE PROFIT IMPROVEMENT.

text.p: Magazine publisher and CD maker PMP Communications Ltd said on Tuesday it expected to see its profit improve in the 1997/98 year after the 17.8 percent fall in net profit to A$47.71 million for the year to June 30, 1997. "Despite this disappointing result we maintain our confidence in the synergies available from the Shomega acquisition and believe we will see solid improvement in earnings in the coming year," PMP said in a statement accompanying its 1996/97 results.
PMP acquired Shomega for A$176 million in June 1996.

"Benefits will be achieved in the form of enhanced sales opportunities and a lower cost structure emanating from plant rationalisation and a reduction in the workforce (which has already been downsized by over 500 people or 10 percent)."
PMP said in addition, fiscal 1998 results will benefit from a more subdued magazine launch programme after it spent over A$4.5 million on unsuccessful launches in fiscal 1997.
This confidence in the earnings prospects was reflected in the final dividend payment which was declared at 10 cents per share, unchanged from a year earlier, PMP said.
At 3.25 p.m. (O525 GMT), PMP shares were 10 cents up at A$3.15.

PMP said paper prices, which had been so volatile in fiscal 1995 and 1996 have been stable for twelve months. This is steadily restoring confidence and encouraging demand for printed advertising material.
"Despite our long term aspiration to establish ourselves in the dynamic Asian market, Pac-Rim Asia continued to perform below expectations," PMP said.

The carrying value of PMP's investment in P.T. Kwartanusa Printing in Indonesia was written down as an abnormal expense of A$4.8 million after tax, having incurred operating losses of A$5.8 million during the period, it said.
PMP said overall during fiscal 1997, A$59 million was invested in new plant and equipment, business acquisitions, and Shomega restructuring costs in excess of that provided at June 30, 1996.
This investment was a reduction on levels of the past three years but pushed gearing (percentage of interest hearing debt to equity) up to 75 percent, PMP said.

"A lower cost base, strong free cashflows from operations, leverage to any improvement in Australian economic activity, and a restrained capital expenditure outlook will result in restoration of gearing to targeted levels," it said.
